1:
Ellicott notes that the Greek is participial and hangs the instruction on the earlier commands to citizens and to slaves, so that the wives are being told to submit in the same way; and he raises at once the question whether this binds Christian wives for all time as completely, since the special reason here was to allay the suspicions raised by a religion that proclaimed the freedom of the individual, and the same apostle's injunction of absolute submission in slaves has since seen slavery abolished altogether. Robertson keeps closer to the wording, observing that the possessive is strengthened by the article, so that wives are enjoined to submit to their own husbands and not to other women's. Calvin sees the point of the paragraph in the harder case, since those married to unbelievers might seem to have a pretence for shaking off the yoke, and argues from the greater to the less: if wives must obey ungodly husbands, much more promptly should those obey who have believing ones. Henry frames it the same way, that conversion to Christ and an interest in Christian privileges do not exempt a woman from subjection to a pagan husband.

How far the prohibition of ornament reaches is the sharpest disagreement in the chapter. Wesley reads it strictly: three things are here expressly forbidden, curling the hair, wearing gold by way of ornament, and putting on costly or gay apparel, and these therefore ought never to be allowed by Christians, much less defended. Calvin raises the question and answers it the other way, that if the words were pressed they would prohibit precious things altogether, whereas what is condemned is excess. Gill says the same, that clothing is both convenient and necessary and a decent modest garb suitable to a person's years and rank is commendable, the fault lying in luxury and immoderation. Barnes goes further still and denies that God condemns real ornament at all, the universe being full of it in the colours of clouds and rainbow, the hues of flowers and the plumage of birds, so that the only question is what the true ornament is. Ellicott shifts the ground entirely, holding that the passage is not directly a corrective of vanity but an answer to a practical question, how the husbands are to be won — not by external prettiness but by character.

Clarke fills in the practice being described, that plaiting the hair and folding it about the head was the most ancient and simplest way of disposing of it, still current across the east and known from gems and statues among Greeks and Romans, and he points to a bust of the wife of Germanicus for a specimen. Robertson notes that the word for adorning is the old sense of ornament rather than the common sense of world, the same double meaning that the Latin word carries. On the contrast that follows, Ellicott resists the received rendering because it makes the hidden man an ornament to be worn instead of gold, which he thinks both illogical and dishonouring; the sense is rather that character and not ornamentation is what wins a husband. Barnes takes incorruptible as the point of comparison, since gold and apparel decay while what pertains to an immortal soul endures. Calvin recalls Cato's remark that those anxious about adorning the body neglect the mind, and Wesley presses the substitution home, that meekness and quietness are put in the room of the ornaments forbidden, since superfluity of dress feeds pride and anger more than is supposed.
5:
The appeal to the past is read as an argument from precedent. Barnes says the point is that this kind of ornament characterised the pious and honoured women of ancient times, those most commended of God, and Ellicott adds that the value God sets on such embellishment is proved by his having accepted it in them. Ellicott presses one word of the translation, since trusted has been substituted for hoped and the position of the holy women was one of expectancy, looking forward to the fulfilment of a promise; and he takes holy to mean not only holy in character but sainted, consecrated by having their memory recorded in Scripture. Robertson notes the tense, that they used to adorn themselves, a customary action. Clarke turns the same verse into a complaint about his own day: simplicity reigned in primitive times and natural ornaments alone were used, until trade and commerce brought in luxuries and luxury brought pride; no female head, he says, looks so well as when adorned with its own hair, which is the ornament appointed by God, and to exchange it for hair of another colour is an insult to the Creator.

On Sarah the commentators agree about the fact and differ about the inference. Calvin observes that the single recorded word is made to stand for a habit, since God does not regard titles and even a petulant wife might say the word once, so that Peter must mean she usually spoke thus, knowing herself commanded to be subject. Ellicott makes the same argument from a subtler angle, that in the one place cited she was not addressing Abraham at all but speaking to herself, and people show their usual habits of mind more freely when they speak to themselves. Barnes and Clarke both cite the rabbinic parallel that reads the passage as Peter does. On the clause about her daughters Ellicott corrects the version sharply: it is not whose daughters ye are but whose children ye became, which points to a definite moment in the past when they came to be what they had not been, and he takes this for evidence that the readers were Gentiles. Clarke reads the same clause as conditional, since the relationship cannot be maintained longer than belief lasts, and belief no longer than obedience. Wesley lists the three adornments the passage names.

The turn to husbands is felt by several to be a correction rather than an addition. Ellicott says the subjection is not to be all one-sided, though the husband's will be of a different kind, and notes that Peter declines to use the word submitting of husbands while conveying the same deference under other terms; he also supposes the case in view to be the mirror of the earlier one, a believing husband with an unbelieving wife, whom he is not to divorce or put away. Calvin requires prudence of them and states the condition plainly, that dominion over wives is given only on terms of exercising authority prudently, so that many foolish and unpleasant things must be borne while taking care that indulgence does not foster folly; and he finds the two reasons given apparently contradictory, honour due because the wife is weak and because she is a joint heir, though they agree well where love exists, since nothing destroys the friendship of life more than contempt. Robertson is careful about the weakness, which is physical and not intellectual or moral. Wesley reads the closing warning as reaching both parties, since all sin hinders prayer and anger particularly.
8:
Calvin uses the turn to general precepts to notice an absence, that among all the particular duties set out for various stations the duty of masters towards their servants is omitted. Some have inferred that there were no Christian masters among the readers, which he rejects, since Paul specifies that duty in letters to Ephesus and Colosse and both cities lay in the region Peter was writing to; the omission is singular but not evidence. Robertson corrects a possible misreading of the opening word, which concludes not the epistle but only the addresses to the various classes, and Wesley agrees that this part runs on into the next chapter, the rest having apparently been added later. Ellicott holds that the general precepts still serve the same purpose as the special ones, since the impression made on unbelieving watchers was the object throughout, and quotes the Lord's word that men will know his disciples by their love for one another. Gill takes the summary as reaching every station named and several not named, magistrates and subjects, masters and servants, parents and children, old and young, rich and poor.

The five words of the list are handled term by term. Robertson observes how unusual they are, three of the five occurring nowhere else in the New Testament and one being a late and rare compound found in Hippocrates. Clarke renders them in order as sympathetic, lovers of the brethren, tender-hearted so that the bowels yearn over the afflicted, and friendly-minded; but he reports that the last is probably not the true reading, since a long list of manuscripts and versions gives humble-minded instead, a reading Griesbach admitted into the text. Robertson silently follows the same reading. Wesley defines the disputed virtue rather than disputing it, calling courtesy such behaviour toward equals and inferiors as shows respect mixed with love, and glosses the sympathy as rejoicing and sorrowing together. Barnes takes the first word to aim at harmony of views and feelings, and Henry at unanimity in the great points of faith, in real affection and in Christian practice, noting that many of the readers were then in a suffering condition, which is why compassion and pity stand in the list at all.

The quotation that follows is agreed to come from the psalm, and the interest is in how it has been altered. Clarke says the words are taken as they stand in the Greek version with the imperatives changed from second person to third, and reduces the passage to five practical rules: refrain from evil speaking and slander, avoid flattery and fair speeches that cover wicked intentions, keep going away from evil, do good, and live peaceably with all men, seeking peace where it has been lost and restoring it where broken. Ellicott finds a deliberate change of sense rather than a lapse of memory, since the psalmist asked merely who desires to live and promised length of days, while the apostle asks who cares to have a life worth having. Barnes observes that neither writer shows any disapproval of the desire for long life, the way to secure it being simply shown. Calvin admits that common feeling favours the opposite, men supposing they expose themselves to insolence if they do not boldly defend themselves, but the Spirit promises a happy life only to the meek and to those who endure evils.
13:
Robertson notes that the sentence is framed as a remote possibility, a rare construction using a mood already dying out of the language, so that the meaning is if matters should after all come to actual suffering. Ellicott presses the same point about the vocabulary, since suffering here is much more than the harm just spoken of and means the horrors of capital punishment, mentioned neither as something already happening nor as certainly impending but as a case well supposable. On the blessedness Robertson observes that the word is the very one used in the beatitude and means happy. Barnes is careful about what is claimed: not that they would find positive enjoyment in persecution, but that they should regard the condition as blessed because favourable to salvation, and so not on the whole an evil. Clarke finds the happiness in the cause rather than the experience, since a man who was not holy would not be persecuted at all. Calvin adds the prior point that kindness does more towards a quiet life than violence and quickness to revenge, so that the blessing belongs to those who suffer after neglecting nothing for peace.

The next clause divides the corpus on a point of text, and the consequences are large. Ellicott states that the right reading, without a shadow of doubt, is sanctify the Lord the Christ in your hearts rather than the Lord God, and draws the inference at once: the words in the prophet name the Lord of hosts, and he asks how a Jew like Peter could ever come to apply them to a man he had known familiarly, except on the supposition that the church's doctrine states a fact. Robertson agrees the correct text reads Christ as Lord and calls the verse an adaptation of the prophet to Christ. Barnes and Clarke work from the older reading and take the difficulty differently. Barnes glosses it from the prophet as regarding God as protector and fearing him rather than what man can do; Clarke asks what sanctifying God can possibly mean, since to sanctify is to make holy and God cannot be made so, and answers that the sense is to entertain just notions of him and to separate him in the heart from everything earthly, human, fickle, rigidly severe or capriciously merciful. Gill takes it as declaring and proclaiming his holiness, as the seraphim did.

On the answer to be given, Robertson recovers the old force of the word, which means a defence rather than an excuse, an answer back of the kind a man makes in court. Calvin adds the qualification that keeps the command from becoming indiscriminate: Peter does not bid us assert and proclaim everywhere, always and to all alike, since the Lord gives his people a spirit of discretion by which they may know when and how far and to whom it is expedient to speak, and bids them only be ready. Henry keeps the two conditions together, that we should be able to defend our religion with meekness and in the fear of God, and observes that where this great fear is there is no room for other fears, since it does not disturb. He takes the good conscience as an office well discharged, and states the comparison of the last verse plainly: it is better to suffer for well-doing than for evil-doing, whatever our natural impatience may suggest at the time, since the man on whom sin and suffering meet together is in a sad condition, sin making the suffering extreme and comfortless and destructive.
18:
The appeal to Christ's suffering is read as an argument from precedent before it is read as doctrine. Ellicott quotes Leighton, that it is some known ease to the mind in distress to look on examples of the like or greater distress, and that the example of Christ weighs more than all the rest together; he notes too that Peter writes King Messiah here rather than Jesus, so that the question becomes whether one who clung to the promises should shrink from a test the Messiah himself endured. Barnes reads the whole passage as governed by that purpose, the reference to Christ's sufferings leading into a statement of the various ways he suffered and of his final triumph, offered to men whose religion exposed them to sorrow. Calvin adds a second comfort drawn from the design rather than the fact of that death, that Christ suffered to bring us to God, so that we are consecrated to him and cannot consistently suffer for our own evil deeds. Henry sets out the same case in stages, that Christ was not exempted from suffering though he had no guilt and could have declined it, and that in his case the just suffered for the unjust by substitution.

The verse about the spirits in prison is the hardest in the epistle and the corpus does not conceal it. Robertson reports that Luther admitted he did not know what Peter means, and then lists the escapes attempted: a conjecture going back to Griesbach that the original text read Noah also, or Enoch also, taken up by a series of modern scholars and admitted into one printed text and one modern translation, though there is no manuscript for it and one editor rejects it as inconsistent with the context. Ellicott sets out the two main lines of interpretation, one making the spirits imprisoned now because they rejected a preaching addressed to them while still on earth, the other making the preaching itself take place after Christ's death; and he decides the sense of the preceding phrase in favour of the second, taking in spirit to mean out of the body, as a disembodied spirit. Clarke holds the first line firmly, that the preaching was by the ministry of Noah over a hundred and twenty years, and that the antediluvians are called imprisoned because, tried and convicted, they were detained under the arrest of divine justice awaiting either repentance or the expiry of their respite.

Wesley and Gill take Clarke's line without his apparatus, Wesley making the preaching Noah's ministry and the prison the reserve of divine justice until sentence was executed, Gill adding that Christ preached by his Spirit in Noah to men who would not believe that a flood would ever come. Calvin rejects one reading before offering his own: the common opinion has found a descent into hell here, but the words say no such thing, since no mention is made of Christ's soul but only that he went by the Spirit, and those are very different things. He then admits the real difficulty, that the verse names not the faithful but only the unbelieving, which appears to overturn his exposition; some have therefore made the passage say that the unbelieving who persecuted the godly found the Spirit of Christ an accuser, but he answers from the next chapter, where the gospel is said to have been preached to the dead that they might live according to God in the spirit, which applies peculiarly to the faithful. Ellicott observes that the word disobedient does not describe all sinners but those who heard and were convinced and still refused.
21:
What the relative pronoun refers back to has to be settled before anything else, and the answers are grammatical. Barnes reports variant readings and rules that the antecedent is clearly not the ark but the water, so that as Noah was saved by water there is a sense in which water is instrumental in our salvation. Clarke reaches the same result through Macknight and by gender, since the relative is neuter and cannot agree with the feminine word for ark but does agree with the neuter word for water. Calvin thinks the case itself has been corrupted and that the relative ought to be read in the dative, though the meaning is not thereby made ambiguous: Noah, saved by water, had a sort of baptism. Ellicott finds two undoubted false readings in the received sentence, the easier whereunto standing where the harder which belongs, and us where the text has you; and he prefers to make the water rather than the baptism the subject, partly from the order of the Greek and partly because of the difficulty of calling the Flood point-blank a baptism. Robertson notes that the word for antitype occurs only once elsewhere.

On what the saving amounts to they are agreed and emphatic. Robertson says the salvation by baptism here is only symbolic, a metaphor or picture, not actual, as Peter hastens to explain in the next clause. Henry states the distinction as the apostle's own guard against mistake: not the outward ceremony of washing, which in itself does no more than put away the filth of the flesh, but the baptism in which there is a faithful answer of a resolved good conscience, engaging to believe in and be devoted to God while renouncing the flesh, the world and the devil — washing being the visible sign and this the thing signified. Wesley says the same, that it is not the bare outward sign but the inward grace, a consciousness that our persons and our actions are accepted. Gill lists the correspondences that make the ark a figure at all: it was God's ordinance and not man's invention, as baptism is of heaven and not of men; it was the scorn of men while it was preparing, as this ordinance still is; and Noah shut into it represented a burial. Calvin makes the burial the point, since in baptism we are buried with Christ.

Ellicott reads the last verse as partly a doxology and finds two purposes in it: it carries the history forward in order, the passion, the death, the activity among the dead, the resurrection, the ascension and the perpetual session following one another, and it teaches the entire conformity of the believer to his Lord, who may hope for a similar experience if he keeps his good conscience. Barnes gives the same encouragement as the reason for mentioning the exaltation at all, since Jesus was reviled and rejected and put to death and yet was raised to the highest honour in the universe, so that the persecuted might hope to come off triumphant. Calvin takes the two clauses as answering two temptations, the ascension commended lest our eyes seek Christ in the world and the session lest we doubt his power to save, since sitting at the right hand means exercising supreme power everywhere as God's representative. Clarke and Ellicott both report a curious addition after that clause in the Latin and some other versions and in several Latin fathers, swallowing up death that we might be made heirs of eternal life, which Clarke notes is in no Greek copy at all.
